frozen_original.title: Kushner Omits 100+ Foreign Contacts on Security Clearance Form SF-86
frozen_original.synopsis: In May 2017, it was revealed that Jared Kushner had filed an initial SF-86 security clearance application that omitted more than 100 foreign contacts, including meetings with Russian Ambassador Sergey Kislyak and the head of a Russian state bank under U.S. sanctions. Kushner's lawyers characterized the omissions as an accident caused by submitting the form prematurely, but career security officials viewed the incomplete disclosure as disqualifying. The form was amended multiple times as additional contacts came to light. The sheer volume of omissions — more than a hundred foreign contacts — stretched credulity that the errors were innocent, particularly given that many of the omitted contacts had direct bearing on the FBI's counterintelligence investigation.

primary.title: Kushner's Initial SF-86 Omitted Foreign-Government Contacts
primary.description_short: Kushner's initial SF-86 omitted foreign-government contacts; the 100+ figure was reported later.
primary.description_medium: Jared Kushner’s initial SF-86 was submitted on January 18, 2017, and omitted foreign-government contacts, according to his later statement and his lawyer’s comments to Politico. He said supplemental information followed the next day. The figure of more than 100 contacts was reported in July 2017, so it does not belong to the record’s May 25 date.
primary.description_long: Jared Kushner submitted his initial SF-86 security questionnaire on January 18, 2017. In a July statement to the Senate Judiciary Committee, he said the filing was a rough draft submitted prematurely after his assistant misunderstood a message; the form did not list any foreign-government contacts. He said supplemental information was sent the next day. His explanation is attributed to him and does not independently establish why the form was incomplete. On July 16, Politico quoted Kushner’s attorney Jamie Gorelick saying the original submission omitted all contacts with foreign-government officials and that later materials included more than 100 calls or meetings with representatives of more than 20 countries. That later figure should not be assigned to the May 25 date in the source record: it was reported in July, months after the initial form. This repair dates the event to the January 18 filing and places the 100+ figure in the later supplementation context. The available material establishes the omission and reported correction, but not deliberate concealment, any particular clearance outcome, or the original synopsis’s suggestion that the contacts materially affected the FBI counterintelligence inquiry.

frozen_original.title: Big Beautiful Bill Eliminates SNAP Benefits for Legal Immigrants
frozen_original.synopsis: The Big Beautiful Bill included provisions stripping SNAP food stamp benefits from legal immigrants, including green card holders who had lawfully resided in the United States for years. The change affected hundreds of thousands of people who had immigrated legally and contributed to American society and tax bases. Anti-hunger advocates warned of increased food insecurity among vulnerable immigrant communities. Legal scholars noted the provision punished lawful conduct and could violate equal protection principles.

primary.title: P.L. 119-21 Retains Lawful Permanent Residents on SNAP Eligibility List
primary.description_short: The 2025 law’s SNAP eligibility list expressly includes lawful permanent residents.
primary.description_medium: Public Law 119-21, approved July 4, 2025, rewrote SNAP’s noncitizen eligibility subsection. Its list expressly includes lawful permanent residents, so the claim that the law eliminated SNAP eligibility for green-card holders generally is inaccurate. The accessed statutory text does not establish the number affected or verify the supplied note about the existing five-year bar.
primary.description_long: On July 4, 2025, Public Law 119-21 amended section 6(f) of the Food and Nutrition Act of 2008, SNAP’s eligibility provision. The amendment lists who may qualify: U.S. citizens or nationals; lawful permanent residents; people granted Cuban and Haitian entrant status; and people lawfully residing under a Compact of Free Association. It also says an individual must be a U.S. resident and a household must otherwise qualify under section 6. Because lawful permanent residents appear expressly in the enacted list, the claim that the law eliminated SNAP eligibility for green-card holders generally is inaccurate. The text does not establish how many people lost eligibility or the effects on food access, and this card makes no numerical impact claim. The supplied research note says a prior five-year bar continues to apply to some lawful permanent residents, but I did not verify that detail in the text accessed here, so it is excluded from the asserted description. The source resolves the title’s blanket statement; it does not by itself establish every category that lost eligibility compared with prior law.

SEC. 10108. ALIEN SNAP ELIGIBILITY.

    Section 6(f) of the Food and Nutrition Act of 2008 (7 U.S.C.

    ``(f) No individual who is a member of a household otherwise

under this section shall be eligible to participate in the supplemental 
nutrition assistance program as a member of that or any other household 
unless he or she is--
            ``(1) a resident of the United States; and
            ``(2) either--
                    ``(A) a citizen or national of the United States;
                    ``(B) an alien lawfully admitted for permanent 
                residence as an immigrant as defined by sections 
                101(a)(15) and 101(a)(20) of the Immigration and 
                Nationality Act, excluding, among others, alien 
                visitors, tourists, diplomats, and students who enter 
                the United States temporarily with no intention of 
                abandoning their residence in a foreign country;
                    ``(C) an alien who has been granted the status of 
                Cuban and Haitian entrant, as defined in section 501(e) 
                of the Refugee Education Assistance Act of 1980 (Public 
                Law 96-422); or
                    ``(D) an individual who lawfully resides in the 
                United States in accordance with a Compact of Free 
                Association referred to in section 402(b)(2)(G) of the 
                Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity 
                Reconciliation Act of 1996.
        The income (less, at State option, a pro rata share) and 
        financial resources of the individual rendered ineligible to 
        participate in the supplemental nutrition assistance program 
        under this subsection shall be considered in determining the 
        eligibility and the value of the allotment of the household of 
        which such individual is a member.''.

    Section 6(f) of the Food and Nutrition Act of 2008 (7 U.S.C. 
2015(f)) is amended to read as follows:
    ``(f) No individual who is a member of a household otherwise 
eligible to participate in the supplemental nutrition assistance program 
under this section shall be eligible to participate in the supplemental 
nutrition assistance program as a member of that or any other household 
unless he or she is--
            ``(1) a resident of the United States; and
            ``(2) either--
                    ``(A) a citizen or national of the United States;
                    ``(B) an alien lawfully admitted for permanent 
                residence as an immigrant as defined by sections 
                101(a)(15) and 101(a)(20) of the Immigration and 
                Nationality Act, excluding, among others, alien 
                visitors, tourists, diplomats, and students who enter 
                the United States temporarily with no intention of 
                abandoning their residence in a foreign country;
                    ``(C) an alien who has been granted the status of 
                Cuban and Haitian entrant, as defined in section 501(e) 
                of the Refugee Education Assistance Act of 1980 (Public 
                Law 96-422); or
                    ``(D) an individual who lawfully resides in the 
                United States in accordance with a Compact of Free 
                Association referred to in section 402(b)(2)(G) of the 
                Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity 
                Reconciliation Act of 1996.
        The income (less, at State option, a pro rata share) and 
        financial resources of the individual rendered ineligible to 
        participate in the supplemental nutrition assistance program 
        under this subsection shall be considered in determining the 
        eligibility and the value of the allotment of the household of 
        which such individual is a member.''.

The amendment lists who may qualify: U.S. citizens or nationals; lawful permanent residents; people granted Cuban and Haitian entrant status; and people lawfully residing under a Compact of Free Association. It also says an individual must be a U.S. resident and a household must otherwise qualify under section 6. Because lawful permanent residents appear expressly in the enacted list, the claim that the law eliminated SNAP eligibility for green-card holders generally is inaccurate. The text does not establish how many people lost eligibility or the effects on food access, and this card makes no numerical impact claim. The supplied research note says a prior five-year bar continues to apply to some lawful permanent residents, but I did not verify that detail in the text accessed here, so it is excluded from the asserted description. The source resolves the title’s blanket statement; it does not by itself establish every category that lost eligibility compared with prior law.
